name: Rasterization and Hardware Primitives
text:
# Rasterization and Hardware Primitives


## Overview
This family renders isosurfaces by converting volume data or [implicit fields](#1800-implicit-surface-primitives.md) into geometric primitives (triangles, quads, or points) and leveraging the GPU's fixed-function rasterization pipeline for depth testing and fragment shading. It differs from sibling methods that perform explicit [ray marching](#6739-ray-marching.md) or binary search within the fragment shader by offloading the heavy lifting of occlusion culling and pixel coverage to hardware, typically at the cost of geometric approximation or specific shading limitations.

## Shared principles
The family shares a core mechanism: for each pixel, a ray is constructed from the camera through the pixel center into the volume domain. The ray is sampled at discrete intervals (marching) or via [acceleration](#18-acceleration.md) structures until the scalar field value $f(\mathbf{p})$ satisfies the isosurface condition, typically $f(\mathbf{p}) \ge \tau$ or a sign change $f(\mathbf{p}_1) \cdot f(\mathbf{p}_2) < 0$ relative to an isovalue $\tau$ [S3, unofficial][S1, unofficial]. Upon detection, the intersection position is often refined (e.g., via linear interpolation or binary search) to reduce discretization artifacts [S3, unofficial][S6, unofficial]. The surface normal is computed from the gradient $\nabla f$ at the hit point, usually via finite differences or tri-cubic filtering, to enable Phong-like shading [S3, unofficial][S1, unofficial]. The final color is computed using local [lighting models](#2056-lighting-models.md) (ambient, diffuse, specular) and potentially ambient occlusion or shadows, with no contribution from voxels behind the surface [S3, unofficial][S5, unofficial].

## Subtopics

### [Multiple Flat Shaded Opaque Isosurfaces](1498-multiple-flat-shaded-opaque-isosurfaces.md)
This method renders [multiple flat-shaded opaque isosurfaces](#1498-multiple-flat-shaded-opaque-isosurfaces.md) from an unstructured tetrahedral mesh without requiring visibility sorting of the cells [1498-multiple-flat-shaded-opaque-isosurfaces]. It solves the problem of correct occlusion and [transparency handling](#3611-order-independent-transparency-approaches.md) in joint rendering by using a texture map to extract isosurface fragments and combining the alpha test with the OpenGL z-test [1498-multiple-flat-shaded-opaque-isosurfaces]. Unlike sibling methods that may rely on geometric sorting or [point rendering](#2827-point-based-rendering.md), this approach leverages hardware rasterization features to handle multiple isovalues simultaneously, though it is limited to flat shading due to the lack of interpolated gradients [1498-multiple-flat-shaded-opaque-isosurfaces].

### [Upson-Keller Polygon Method](2041-upson-keller-polygon-method.md)
The [Upson-Keller Polygon Method](#2041-upson-keller-polygon-method.md) is an early image-order volume rendering technique that renders isosurfaces by intersecting scan planes with volume elements to form polygons, which are then rasterized using fixed-function hardware features like alpha-testing and stencil buffers. It differs from sibling methods such as [Multiple Flat Shaded Opaque Isosurfaces](1498-multiple-flat-shaded-opaque-isosurfaces.md) by explicitly managing front-to-back opacity integration via span-based accumulation rather than simple depth-buffered occlusion, and from [OpenGL Point Rendering for Isosurfaces](8433-opengl-point-rendering-for-isosurfaces.md) by using polygonal spans instead of point sprites.

### [OpenGL Point Rendering for Isosurfaces](8433-opengl-point-rendering-for-isosurfaces.md)
Rendering isosurfaces using OpenGL point primitives (GL_POINTS) instead of triangles, where points are rendered as discs. This method is prone to being fill-rate limited because points overlap to cover the surface and cannot be backface culled.

### Hardware Rasterization
#### definition
- [S1, unofficial] Replaces the [CUDA](#3671-dual-contouring-2d-cuda.md) software rasterizer with a GPU hardware rasterizer to separate pipeline overhead from primitive efficiency.
#### step
- [S1, unofficial] Port the rendering pipeline to Vulkan; sort surfels globally instead of per tile; draw each primitive as a quad through the graphics pipeline.
#### pitfall
- [S1, unofficial] Quality-wise, the GPU hardware rasterizer matches the CUDA software rasterizer on all 13 scenes, with at most 0.05 dB and 0.0007 LPIPS deviation.
#### number
- [S1, unofficial] Mean frame rates rise to 2698, 3016, and 4413 [FPS](#7182-farthest-point-sampling-fps.md) on [Mip-NeRF 360](#3306-mip-nerf-360.md), Tanks & Temples, and Deep Blending, respectively, representing a 1.8× speedup over the CUDA implementation.
- [S1, unofficial] 77% of fragments generated by the hardware rasterizer survive support and opacity tests on average (53–86% across 13 scenes), compared to 17% for software tile evaluation.

## Background
The use of hardware rasterization for volume isosurfaces dates back to the early days of 3D graphics acceleration, where the [Upson-Keller method](#1968-cell-projection-with-scan-line-conversion.md) (1985) pioneered the use of scan-line intersection and stencil buffers to render isosurfaces from voxel data [S2, unofficial]. This approach allowed for real-time [interaction](#41-interaction.md) with volumetric data before dedicated volume ray-casting hardware existed. Modern implementations, such as those utilizing hardware rasterization for [splatting](#23-splatting.md) or mesh-based isosurfaces, continue to leverage the efficiency of the fixed-function pipeline for occlusion culling, as seen in recent [ultrafast spatial texture-atlas splatting](#3245-ultrafast-spatial-texture-atlas-splatting.md) techniques [S1, unofficial].
